# Faroe Islands company registration and annual reporting v0.3
> **Checked against the law.** This Guide prepares working papers for review. It has no professional attestation and does not authorise a filing, incorporation or payment.
## What this file is and scope

Prepare the formation, ownership, accounting-framework and filing calendar for an ordinary P/F or Sp/F. Keep company registration, TAKS registration and each tax obligation separate. P/F and Sp/F owners have the limited liability stated in Companies Act §1; that does not remove management duties or pre-registration liability. Sole traders, partnerships, ÍVF, foundations, regulated entities, foreign branches, reorganisations, licences and insolvency advice require their own rules. [Companies Act §§1–4, 41][company]

**Period first.** Annual Accounts Act 206 of 12 December 2025 takes effect on 1 January 2026 for **financial years beginning on or after that date**. It repeals Order 1355/2007 and preserves implementing rules until replaced or repealed. Accounts for a financial year beginning in 2025 do not become 2026-framework accounts merely because they are filed in 2026. Use the prior Act for that earlier period. The new law's actual title says **206**, although its official URL contains **203**. [2025 Act §203][accounts]; [prior Act][prior]
## Formation and registration

1. **Identify founders, name and governance.** One or more founders are permitted; test capacity and the statutory insolvency/guardianship restrictions. Use the correct P/F or Sp/F suffix and check the proposed name against §2. A P/F has a board/executive or supervisory/executive structure, with at least three on its board or supervisory body. An Sp/F can use executive management, subject to the employee-representation exception. Record the selected structure, office holders and authority. [Companies Act §§2, 24, 111][company]

2. **Execute documents.** All founders sign the formation document, including articles. Record founders, subscription price, subscription/payment deadlines, legal and accounting effective dates and any formation costs borne by the company. Articles state name, objects, capital/shares and rights, management, general-meeting notice and financial year. Add §27's special-benefit, asset-contribution and audit-election provisions where applicable. [Companies Act §§25–29][company]

3. **Evidence capital.** Apply the table below to subscribed capital, cash actually paid and premium separately. Noncash assets must have economic value; promised work/services and claims against founders/shareholders do not qualify. Obtain an independent valuation report, ordinarily dated no more than four weeks before signature, unless a verified §38 exception and management report apply. [Companies Act §§31–38][company]

4. **Register on time.** Incorporation must be registered or notified to Skráseting Føroya within two weeks after signature; late formation cannot simply be registered under that document. Evidence the capital payment by registration/notification. Where management/auditor was not elected at formation, §39 requires the relevant meeting within two weeks. Register office holders and any auditor; retain authority and valid evidence for the filer. [Companies Act §§9–10, 15, 39–40][company]

5. **Open the correct operational records.** Prepare the shareholder register and ownership notifications. The Registrar formation page supplies the current notification and owner forms; it says the owner notification accompanies the formation papers. An unregistered company uses the statutory “under formation” designation; persons making or sharing responsibility for pre-registration commitments have the joint liability in §41. A future legal effective date has separate restrictions. [Companies Act §§41, 50–58b][company]; [Registrar forms page][forms]

6. **Complete TAKS onboarding.** TAKS's published starting-business procedure asks for the Vinnuskráin form at least eight days before activity, plus the articles, formation document and shareholder register for a limited company. Registrar notification to TAKS does not prove that the tax/business-register file is complete. Retain the V-tal and tax-registration decisions. A V-tal alone does not prove MVG registration. Owners' company salary follows A-income settlement; use the payroll Guide. [TAKS, Registering a company and Taxation][start]

## Ownership and recurring management duties

Maintain the shareholder register promptly after formation, with identity, holdings, acquisition/disposal/pledge dates and voting rights. Foreign holders require unambiguous identity evidence. Shareholder/pledgee notification of an ownership or pledge change reaches the company within two weeks. Significant legal owners notify the company within two weeks after crossing a §55 boundary. At formation, register significant owners, or the absence of such owners, with the Registrar at the latest simultaneously with formation; later threshold changes are notified as soon as possible. These records are distinct from beneficial-owner registration. [Companies Act §§50–58][company]

Identify the natural persons who ultimately own or control, directly, indirectly or by other means, under §5(30). **At formation, collect and register the beneficial-owner information and rights no later than simultaneously with company registration under §58b.** This initial deadline is separate from the later-awareness/update rule. Do not automatically reuse the 5% legal-owner threshold or import an unverified fixed beneficial-owner percentage. Obtain the control chain and rights; §58a requires prompt registration after awareness and prompt updates. If all identification possibilities have been exhausted and there is no identifiable beneficial owner, register the prescribed daily management, with the failed-identification evidence. Review beneficial-owner information **at least annually**, presenting the result at the management meeting approving the annual report. Preserve beneficial-owner evidence for five years after that ownership ends, and identification-attempt evidence for five years after the attempts. [Companies Act §§5(30), 58a–58b][company]

If equity is established to be below half subscribed capital, management must hold a general meeting within six months of that finding, explain the position and propose necessary measures. This capital-loss duty is separate from whether cash remains or an annual filing is due. Keep the finding date and action record. [Companies Act §119][company]
## Accounts, audit and separate deadlines

For the new-law period, document class under §7 before choosing the report. Class B's ordinary minimum includes management statement (subject to the one-person exception), balance sheet, profit and loss, notes and management report; include any required audit/assurance report. Class C adds equity and cash-flow statements. Use a consistent framework and accounting policies, accrual recognition and the statutory true-and-fair requirement. This checklist does not supply every recognition/disclosure rule. [Annual Accounts Act §§9–16, 25, 80][accounts]

B/C/D ordinarily require an approved auditor's audit. Test each lawful opt-out or extended-review alternative, the two years and any mandatory override. The new law has the separate DKK 50m assets override, foundation and holding/influence provisions, and disqualifications for specified offences, bankruptcy bans and Registrar findings. A size pass alone is insufficient. Check the formation/annual-meeting resolution, articles, management declarations and registered auditor status. Only an auditor approved under Faroese law can give the assurance prescribed by §158; this Guide makes no licence-equivalence claim. [Companies Act §§27, 88][company]; [Annual Accounts Act §§10–11, 156–158][accounts]

## Enforcement, retention and output checks

Late Registrar accounts are not cured by submitting the tax return. New-law §177 provides a demand with at least eight working days to comply and a separate four-week point after which the Registrar can seek dissolution or use the applicable removal route. If accounts arrive after the demand's compliance period, §178 permits a charge for **each** relevant manager/branch manager: DKK 500 for the first commenced month, **cumulative** DKK 2,000 for the second, DKK 3,000 for the third, capped at DKK 3,000 each, calculated from the original filing deadline. The amounts are not DKK 500 + DKK 2,000 + DKK 3,000. Section 179 addresses exceptional relief; blaming staff/advisers does not by itself relieve the manager. Prior §§150–151 provide the corresponding earlier-period demand/charge route. [Annual Accounts Act §§177–179][accounts]; [prior Act §§150–151][prior]

Compulsory-dissolution restoration is conditional, not an automatic late fee. Companies Act §§231–232 require correction, management/auditor and capital evidence and the prescribed resolutions/notifications. The Registrar must receive the restoration notification within three months after asking the court for compulsory dissolution, subject to the restructuring suspension; prior compulsory dissolution within five years and a final dissolution decision prevent the ordinary restoration route. Obtain insolvency advice for an actual case. [Companies Act §§231–232][company]

Bookkeeping must preserve both original and corrected entries, link transactions to documents and accounts and reconcile balances. Retain accounting material safely for **five years from financial-year end**, accessible and reproducible. Electronic foreign storage has the conditions in §14, including access in the Faroes and local system/password descriptions; paper has distinct location exceptions. Management departure or business closure does not end retention. Statutory five-year retention is not an instruction to destroy records with another continuing purpose. [Bookkeeping Act §§6–17][books]

Deliver the signed-formation/document index, paid/subscribed-capital reconciliation, shareholder and beneficial-owner schedules, framework/audit decision paper, separate filing calendar and receipt log. Check:
- Every threshold uses the correct financial-year start and current law for that period.
- Capital payment, premium and noncash evidence reconcile; no incorporation fee is invented.
- Legal-owner and beneficial-owner records use their own tests, dates and retention clocks.
- Two-year size tests, elections, group/holding overrides and disqualifications have evidence.
- Accounts approval and Registrar/tax receipts are distinct; event deadlines are not replaced by the annual cycle.
- Retention and unresolved questions are handed to the reviewer.

# Faroe Islands corporate income tax v0.6
## Who this applies to

This Guide prepares ordinary and separate capital-income tax working papers for Faroese P/F and Sp/F companies. Faroese registration brings companies with limited-liability participants within Tax Act §1(1)(8); §1(2) also covers relevant foreign-registered entities whose effective management is in the Faroes. Treaty residence requires separate analysis. [Tax Act][tax]

Compute ordinary income and non-business capital gains in separate schedules. Business securities activity belongs in ordinary income under Capital Income Act §3; company interest and negative interest belong there under §10(1). The separate §14 calculation covers the remaining statutory capital items. Do not classify every investment receipt as ordinary income or every company interest receipt as separate capital income. [Capital Income Act §§1–4, 10, 14][capital]

Petroleum, fishing/resource charges, aquaculture surcharges, tonnage taxation, reorganisations and minimum-tax exposure need separate work. Identify those activities before using the ordinary calculation. An 18% result here is not necessarily the company's complete tax liability.

**Period:** income year 2026, with the additions below checked on 28 October 2026 against retained current primary provisions and the stated TAKS guidance. Earlier source checks retain their dates. The Tax Act consolidation identifies amendment 53 of 1 June 2026, effective 1 September 2026. Event-specific rules must be matched to the event date.

## The base

Start with a reconciled trial balance and a separate tax-adjustment schedule. Operating expenditure incurred to earn, secure and maintain income is addressed by Tax Act §31. Tax depreciation is governed separately, so an accounting depreciation charge is not its own tax deduction. Business loan interest, specified financing fees and negative interest fall under §33(1)(1). Interest deducted when due but still unpaid at the end of the following income year is brought back into the original due-year income, subject to the provision's bank-credit payment test. Check related-party restrictions under §37b before allowing it. Assets acquired for resale or within the taxpayer's trading business require Tax Act §27 treatment; property held for less than two years carries a rebuttable resale-profit presumption. Ordinary unrealised asset changes are excluded under §29(2), subject to its exceptions. [Tax Act][tax]
Working-paper sequence:
1. Identify the entity, period and applicable rate provision.
2. Reconcile revenue, costs and accounting profit to signed accounts and ledgers.
3. Separate ordinary income from capital-income items and special regimes; document the legal classification for each material item.
4. Reverse accounting charges that require separate tax treatment; insert only deductions supported by the applicable law and schedules.
5. Establish the allowable loss balance, then apply it against positive ordinary taxable income. Preserve the unused balance by origin year and entity.
6. Multiply the resulting ordinary taxable income by the established rate. Reconcile the assessment and actual payment notices separately.
### Ordinary business equipment depreciation

For machinery, furniture and similar equipment used exclusively in the business, maintain a tax pool separately from accounting carrying values. Classify assets first: buildings, leased-premises installations, ships, mixed/private-use assets and passenger cars subject to §5a cannot simply be placed in this ordinary equipment calculation. Foreign-managed joint ownership also has §1 restrictions. [Depreciation Act §§1–2, 5a][depreciation]

For an ordinary positive pool, start with the opening tax balance, add qualifying acquisitions and deduct disposal proceeds. The maximum annual deduction is **30%** of that adjusted balance. If the balance before depreciation is **DKK 20,000 or less**, the positive remainder can be deducted in full. The ceiling is not a mandatory deduction. [§2(3)–(5)][depreciation]

Separately, an eligible item costing **DKK 20,000 or less** can be deducted immediately in its acquisition year under §3. Choose either full immediate deduction or inclusion of its entire cost in the pool; do not claim both. Subsequent sale proceeds of an immediately deducted item are fully taxable income, not a second pool reduction. [§3(1)–(4)][depreciation]

A proved disposal loss has special treatment: compare proceeds with that asset's cost less prior tax depreciation. Deduct the loss in the disposal year and remove the asset's remaining tax value from the pool. Do not both remove that tax value and deduct the proceeds again from the pool. Keep asset-level records even though ordinary annual depreciation uses a pool. [§4(1)][depreciation]

If proceeds create a negative pool, stop the positive-pool calculation. Section 5 allows inclusion in taxable income in the current year and requires settlement by the following income year unless offset through qualifying acquisitions or a permitted extension. Record the negative balance and its deadline; it is not a negative depreciation deduction. The full reinvestment/extension procedure remains outside this Guide. [§5][depreciation]
### Passenger cars used exclusively for business

Depreciation Act §5a applies to passenger cars used exclusively for business but registered for private passenger transport when acquisition cost **exceeds DKK 150,000**. Registration class and actual use are separate tests. Do not assume a company-owned car qualifies for ordinary pooling merely because its use is entirely business-related. Exactly DKK 150,000 does not trigger this particular above-threshold exclusion; other classification conditions still apply. [§5a(1)][depreciation]

For an affected car, keep a separate DKK 150,000 depreciable balance. Record the excess purchase cost and improvement expenditure as a separate non-depreciable asset item in the accounts accompanying the return. Apply the compatible Chapter 1 rules to the depreciable portion, including the 30% annual ceiling, without adding this car to the ordinary equipment pool. No depreciation is allowed in its disposal year. [§5a(2)–(4), (6)][depreciation]

On disposal, compare proceeds with full acquisition cost plus improvements less prior depreciation. A positive gain is taxable. A loss is deductible only to the extent it exceeds the amount that §5a(2) excluded from depreciation. This differs from deducting the full accounting loss. Preserve original cost, improvements, prior tax deductions and the excluded balance separately. [§5a(4)][depreciation]
### Mixed use, change of use and ships

For equipment used both privately and for business, keep an individual schedule under §7. Compute annual depreciation at an elected whole percentage up to 30% of acquisition cost in year one and unrelieved balance thereafter, subject to the DKK 150,000 acquisition-cost cap. Only the current-year business-use share of that computed depreciation is deductible. Keep both total computed depreciation and actually deducted business depreciation: disposal recapture/loss allocation under §8 uses the ratio of those cumulative amounts, with the statutory excluded-cost restriction. No depreciation is computed in the sale year. Improvements to an asset originally acquired above the cap are also excluded. [Depreciation Act §§7–10][depreciation]

A transfer to exclusively private or mixed use is a deemed sale and purchase at market value under §31. A transfer from exclusively private use into business or mixed use is a deemed purchase at that value. The passenger-car transitions in §5a(5) expressly invoke §31, including the above-DKK-150,000 market-value condition for a Chapter 1 car moving into §5a use. Record the transition date, market evidence, old basis and recapture before opening the new schedule. Employee benefit valuation and payroll reporting are separate from the company asset schedule. Use the payroll Guide’s [dated 2026 benefit values and reporting](fo-payroll-contributions.md#ordinary-benefit-valuation); its stated adjustment/exemption limits remain. [Depreciation Act §§5a(5), 31][depreciation]

Keep a separate commercial ship pool, including equipment used commercially aboard ships; §11 also expressly addresses the specified commercial fishing licences. Chapter 1 rules apply subject to §12, whose pool deducts relevant scrapping subsidies and disposal proceeds. A negative balance must be settled by the following income year unless qualifying replacement acquisitions or permitted extension apply. For contracted decked-ship construction/reconstruction, advance depreciation starts in the contract year, is capped at 15% per year and 45% in total, and continues only until delivery. On delivery, add cost net of advance depreciation to the ship pool. Contract cancellation recaptures prior advance deductions; sale of contract rights has its own gain/loss computation including prior advance deductions. This does not establish eligibility for tonnage tax or fishing levies. [Depreciation Act §§11–16][depreciation]
### Business buildings

Classify each building under Depreciation Act §17 before selecting a rate. Category (a) covers exclusive craft/industrial use, including necessary offices/storage; (b) covers exclusive hotel use or rental buildings with at least ten apartments, including necessary offices/storage. Category (c), including other office/storage buildings, requires at least **75%** business floor area. Residential use is excluded except within the express §17(1) exceptions. [§17][depreciation]

### Purchased goodwill and other business intangibles

Tax Act §35a(2) permits purchased goodwill and other business-use intangible acquisition cost to be deducted in equal amounts in the purchase year and the next nine years. For a right covering a specified term, use equal deductions over that entire term instead. Keep the contract, business-use evidence, purchase price, term and cumulative deductions separately from the equipment pool. A hypothetical DKK 100,000 goodwill purchase gives DKK 10,000 annually over ten years; a DKK 100,000 right lasting five years gives DKK 20,000 annually. These are derived amounts, not statutory allowances per asset. [Tax Act §35a(1)–(2)][tax]

Business intangible sale proceeds enter sale-year income under §35a(1); subsection 3 allows the same asset's undeducted acquisition cost against those proceeds, or deduction in the business-cessation year. For an asset still held, follow subsection 3's ten-year route by reference to subsection 2; cessation and continued holding must be distinguished. Gifts/advances on inheritance and changes between business and private use follow subsection 4's deemed acquisition/disposal and ordinary-market-value rules. Do not replace these with accounting impairment or write off purchased goodwill immediately. [Tax Act §35a(1), (3)–(4)][tax]
### Losses

Section 33a allows forward deduction, using available earlier profits before carrying losses to a later year. Company losses are forfeited if its at-least-50% continuity test for capital or voting value is not met, comparing the beginning of the utilisation year with the end of the loss year. Exactly 50% continuing in the same hands meets the stated numerical boundary. The statute preserves an exception where the company carried on significant business activity involving economic risk when ownership changed. Do not treat every share sale as automatic forfeiture. [§33a(1)–(2)][tax]

Debt cancellation/reduction also reduces losses; debt-to-equity conversion uses the difference between face and market value, with adjustment for debt-release income taxed. Review the transaction before using the old loss balance. [§33a(3)][tax]
### Separate non-business capital-income computation

First test Capital Income Act §3: business-related securities/claim gains and losses enter ordinary taxable income, using realisation and FIFO for equal-right shares unless the taxpayer has made the irrevocable mark-to-market election. Business foreign-exchange gains/losses on claims/debts follow §6(6). Company interest and negative interest are ordinary items under §10(1). Remove those amounts from the separate capital schedule. [Capital Income Act §§3, 6, 10][capital]

For remaining share/securities disposals, compute realised proceeds less acquisition cost using FIFO for equal-right shares in the same company. Fully Faroese-taxable companies/funds reduce a security's allowable disposal loss by exempt dividends received from that security: only the excess loss qualifies. Allotted bonus shares and subscription rights have zero acquisition cost and follow the parent share's acquisition date. Claims, debt and options have their own realised acquisition/disposal or debt-release computations under §§6–8; the DKK 1,000 claim/debt-gain threshold in §6(4) is for individuals/estates, not companies. Debt cancellation under §7 taxes the statutory reduction below the creditor's claim market value, subject to its exception. [§§4, 6–8][capital]

Dividends received by fully Faroese-taxable companies/funds holding share or contributed capital in the distributing company are exempt under §9(1). The text sets no minimum participation percentage or holding period; do not import one. A distribution is broadly defined by §1(2); a final-liquidation-year distribution follows disposal treatment, and capital-reduction distributions need TAKS permission for that treatment. A sale back to the issuer is ordinarily a dividend under §5 unless permission or its specific exceptions apply. Do not grant ordinary capital-loss relief to a gross distribution without checking that classification. [§§1, 5, 9][capital]

Aggregate the separate §14 categories after their own adjustments. Track eligible carried capital losses separately and use them against capital net gains at the first available opportunity. A capital loss cannot reduce ordinary trading profit. Capital Income Act §14(2) allows ordinary-income losses, including eligible carried ordinary losses, to shelter separate capital gain only up to that ordinary loss; record the ordinary loss used once. Apply 18% to the remaining company capital gain. Capital losses have their own §14(4) 50% ownership-continuity/significant-business exception. Do not assume a surviving ordinary-loss balance proves the separate capital-loss balance survives. [§14][capital]; [TAKS][taks]
This produces two reconciled bases, two loss ledgers and the resulting tax, not one undifferentiated accounting-profit calculation. Group ordering requires the next section.
### Group taxation

Regulation 148/2015 requires eligible Faroese-registered entities, matching financial years and full subsidiary ownership throughout the subsidiary's income year. Application is written, ordinarily by 1 July following the first relevant year, with returns/accounts submitted before consideration. Companies in liquidation cannot obtain permission; liquidation ends their participation from that income year. Section 4(4) prohibits renewed permission after departure. Treat approval as evidence, not an assumption. [Regulation §§1–5][group]

Each company computes its own ordinary result under §6(1). Apply the following order before pooling; distinguish pre-group losses, losses arising during grouping, and capital losses by entity and origin year. [Regulation §6][group]

1. Use pre-group ordinary losses against that company's own ordinary surplus (§6(3)). Remaining pre-group losses then shelter its own capital income, after older capital losses (§6(4)); preserve any remainder for that company's later years (§6(5)).

2. Use its own earlier group-period ordinary losses against its own ordinary surplus (§6(6)). Its remaining current/group-period ordinary losses then shelter its own current capital income, after older capital losses and pre-group ordinary losses (§6(7)).

3. Only then allocate the remaining current/group-period ordinary loss, up to the remaining combined ordinary surpluses, proportionally among the surplus companies (§6(8)). For each surplus company, allocation is `usable group loss × its remaining ordinary surplus / total remaining ordinary surpluses`. Preserve unused current/group-period losses for later use under the same ordering (§6(9)). A loss never becomes a transferable pre-group loss merely because a company was acquired.

4. Report the combined ordinary result on the parent's return using the special TAKS group schedule (§6(2)). A departing company retains its own unused pre-group and group-period losses (§7); the parent receives assessments/refunds under §8. Subsection 6(10) confines the stated debt-compromise loss reduction to the debtor company's own loss before the remaining group-period loss is used; obtain its debt/restructuring evidence before applying it.

**Ordinary group control:** assume approved full-year grouping, no ownership-loss forfeiture or debt compromise, no separate capital-group permission, and C as parent. A has ordinary profit DKK 200,000, pre-group loss DKK 40,000 and own old group-period loss DKK 30,000, leaving DKK 130,000. C has DKK 70,000 ordinary profit. B has current ordinary loss DKK 100,000 and capital gain DKK 25,000 less old capital loss DKK 5,000. B first uses DKK 20,000 ordinary loss against its own net capital income; only DKK 80,000 remains for ordinary group allocation. A receives `80,000 × 130,000 / 200,000 = 52,000`; C receives DKK 28,000. Their final ordinary bases are DKK 78,000 and DKK 42,000: total DKK 120,000 and tax DKK 21,600 at the established 18% rate. B has no taxable capital remainder and no unused current ordinary loss in this fixture. [Regulation §6(3)–(9)][group]; [Capital Income Act §14][capital]; [Assessment Act §5(2)][rate]

Under §9 the parent pays B DKK 14,400 compensation for the DKK 80,000 loss used; A pays the parent DKK 9,360 loss compensation and DKK 14,040 for the tax the parent pays for A. C's own loss benefit is DKK 5,040 and its own tax DKK 7,560. The parent's net cash outflow is `21,600 + 14,400 − 9,360 − 14,040 = 12,600`, matching `70,000 × 18%`. These internal payments have no tax consequences and must be paid or booked by 1 October following the income year. Compensation follows the losses actually used, not every available loss balance. [Regulation §9][group]

The ordinary permission does not itself cover capital-income grouping. Capital Income Act §14a provides a separate TAKS permission for Faroese-resident parent/subsidiary companies with the same accounting year and full qualifying ownership. Pre-group losses remain restricted to that company's own surplus. Parent responsibility and participating companies' joint liability follow §14a(3). Obtain the actual capital-group permission and applicable implementing conditions; they remain incomplete here. TAKS's ordinary-group summary must not be read as repealing this distinct statutory route. [Capital Income Act §14a][capital]; [TAKS][taks]
## Deadlines and filing

Company returns are ordinarily due **1 July following the income year** under §100(3). For a calendar-year 2026 company, that means 1 July 2027. A permitted extension cannot exceed **15 August** under §105. [Tax Act][tax]

TAKS requires company accounts with the return, including exempt companies; accounts must be submitted on Borgaragluggin. Retrieve the current return and accounting template and retain submission receipts. [TAKS returns][returns]

Ordinary company tax falls due in three payments on **1 October, 1 November and 1 December**, with payment permitted through the **20th** of each month. Use the assessed year and issued amounts; do not substitute the return deadline for the payment calendar. [Tax Act §81][tax]; [TAKS][taks]

For a new resident company, §21 taxes the whole first accounting period, with the return by 1 July and the statutory October–December payment dates. The first period cannot exceed 18 months, begin before 1 January of the incorporation year, or span more than two calendar years. A cessation or move into exempt activity requires the liquidator/board to notify TAKS and provide the intervening-income statement within four weeks; it does not erase the company's final-year liability. An existing business transferred to a company uses market values unless the separately legislated conversion regime applies. [Tax Act §21][tax]

Report separate capital income digitally or on TAKS's form by the ordinary return deadline. No additional capital form is needed if the issued capital statement is correct and complete. Separate capital assessment tax is due on the first of the month after the statement is issued, payable through the 20th. Additional capital tax of DKK 500 or less is not collected; refunds below DKK 50 are not paid. These are settlement thresholds, not exemptions for gains. [Capital Income Act §18(1)–(3), (6)][capital]

A company declaring dividends pays withheld tax and supplies the recipient/calculation statement within 14 days after the distribution decision. Withhold 35% for individuals/estates and 18% for entities outside the §9(1) exemption, before a verified treaty or specific relief. Retain the decision, recipient identity/status, exemption or relief authority and remittance receipt. Do not substitute a payment-date deadline for the statutory decision-date trigger. [Capital Income Act §§9, 15][capital]
## Penalties and interest

Section 104 provides estimated assessment for a missing timely complete return, a DKK **1,000–5,000** fine, and income-tax increases of **2%** when less than seven days late or **5%** when seven or more days late. Relief requires a supported application under subsection 3. [Tax Act][tax]

Section 81(2) states ordinary late-payment interest of **0.7% per commenced month**, subject to §146(1). That latter provision requires payment of underpaid tax in the specified offence cases and **12% annual interest** for its specified companies from the end of the relevant tax year. Section 146(2) also addresses under-assessment without a punishable offence; do not describe 12% as applying only to deliberate evasion. Do not stack or substitute these mechanically. TAKS's short guidance describes the ordinary calculation from the timely-payment date, whereas §81 says the due date; obtain the assessment's calculation if the start-date distinction affects the charge. [Tax Act][tax]; [TAKS][taks]

Late separate capital returns attract estimated assessment, a DKK 1,000–5,000 fine and the same less-than-seven-day 2% / at-least-seven-day 5% tax increase under Capital Income Act §18(7), subject to the supported relief application. Late capital-assessment or dividend-withholding payment carries 0.7% for each commenced month from the statutory due date, including booked interest as specified; interest is not an ordinary income-tax deduction. [Capital Income Act §§15(4), 18(1), (4), (7)][capital]

Tax Act §139 penalises false/misleading tax information given with evasion intent by fine, detention or imprisonment up to two years; gross negligence has the separate subsection 2 treatment. Section 139b addresses evasion-motivated failure to file, while §140 addresses false/misleading control information. No fixed monetary fine is supplied by those provisions. Keep offence assessment separate from the mechanical late-return increases. [Tax Act §§139–140][tax]
## Cross-border points

Foreign incorporation does not settle residence where effective management is Faroese. Foreign businesses require a separate domestic-source/PE and treaty analysis under §§1–2. Controlled transactions and thin capitalisation require their own schedules; see the transfer-pricing Guide. Foreign-source capital income from a country without a double-tax treaty can receive credit under Capital Income Act §19 for tax actually paid/withheld there, capped at Faroese tax attributable to that same income. Tax Act §154 separately supplies credit for eligible ordinary income from a country without a treaty. Use the [ordinary foreign-tax credit method and its precise limits](fo-cross-border-payments.md#ordinary-foreign-tax-credit), including the source-expense and same-income caps; §19 must not be treated as its statutory substitute. Treaty eligibility, nonpositive credit bases, later adjustments, PE profit attribution and refund procedures remain separate. Cross-border dividends require the domestic §15 starting position above and a recipient-specific treaty/relief review. [Tax Act §§1–2, 37a–37b][tax]; [Capital Income Act §§15, 19][capital]
## Two worked examples that recompute
### 1. Ordinary profit with equipment depreciation

Assume a qualifying 18% company with accounting profit DKK 600,000 after DKK 80,000 accounting depreciation. Its exclusively business-used ordinary equipment pool opens at DKK 200,000; eligible pooled additions are DKK 100,000, with no disposals. Elect the 30% maximum: pool depreciation is DKK 90,000 and the closing pool DKK 210,000. A separate eligible DKK 20,000 item, capitalised and not expensed in that accounting profit, is immediately deducted. Total tax depreciation/deduction is DKK 110,000, ordinary taxable income DKK 570,000 and tax DKK 102,600. Assume no capital items, loss relief, car cap or other adjustments. [Depreciation Act §§2–3][depreciation]; [Assessment Act §5(2)][rate]
```oa-check
name: Faroese company ordinary profit and equipment deductions
inputs:
profit: 600000
accounting_depreciation: 80000
opening_pool: 200000
additions: 100000
separate_small_item: 20000
depreciation_rate: 0.30
tax_rate: 0.18
steps:
pool: opening_pool + additions
pool_depreciation: pool * depreciation_rate
closing_pool: pool - pool_depreciation
tax_deductions: pool_depreciation + separate_small_item
taxable: profit + accounting_depreciation - tax_deductions
tax: taxable * tax_rate
expected:
pool_depreciation: 90000
closing_pool: 210000
tax_deductions: 110000
taxable: 570000
### 2. Capital losses, exempt dividends and an ordinary loss

Assume a standalone fully taxable company with verified ordinary trading loss DKK 150,000 before DKK 30,000 company interest income. Its ordinary loss is therefore DKK 120,000. Separate realised non-business share gains are DKK 240,000. Another security is sold at a DKK 100,000 loss but has paid DKK 60,000 total exempt dividends; §4(3) allows only DKK 40,000 of that loss. The dividends themselves are excluded under §9. The current capital net gain is DKK 200,000, reduced by DKK 50,000 eligible carried capital losses to DKK 150,000. Using the DKK 120,000 ordinary loss once leaves DKK 30,000 taxable capital gain and DKK 5,400 tax. Neither loss balance remains. Assume all classification, FIFO and continuity conditions are satisfied, no group permission, foreign credit or withholding credit, and that none of the securities activity is business activity under §3. [Capital Income Act §§3–4, 9–10, 14][capital]

name: Faroese separate capital result and one-way ordinary loss relief
inputs:
trading_loss: 150000
company_interest: 30000
share_gains: 240000
security_loss: 100000
exempt_dividends_on_security: 60000
carried_capital_loss: 50000
rate: 0.18
steps:
ordinary_loss: max(0, trading_loss - company_interest)
allowed_security_loss: max(0, security_loss - exempt_dividends_on_security)
current_capital_gain: share_gains - allowed_security_loss
capital_loss_used: min(current_capital_gain, carried_capital_loss)
capital_after_own_losses: current_capital_gain - capital_loss_used
ordinary_loss_used: min(capital_after_own_losses, ordinary_loss)
taxable_capital: capital_after_own_losses - ordinary_loss_used
capital_tax: taxable_capital * rate
capital_loss_remaining: carried_capital_loss - capital_loss_used
ordinary_loss_remaining: ordinary_loss - ordinary_loss_used

allowed_security_loss: 40000
current_capital_gain: 200000

ordinary_loss_used: 120000

# Faroe Islands country-by-country reporting v0.2
## Who this applies to

Tax Act §§118b–g govern country-by-country reporting (CbCR). A multinational group operates through constituent entities in more than one tax jurisdiction. The perimeter includes qualifying permanent establishments and entities excluded from consolidation solely for size or materiality. Determine the ultimate parent using the consolidation/control definition, not the group's preferred reporting company. [§118b][law]
This Guide prepares an obligation assessment and reporting workpaper. It does not certify a particular exchange relationship, submit a report, determine transfer prices or calculate minimum tax.

## The base
1. Establish the group perimeter, parent residence, consolidation rules, reporting year and prior-year consolidated revenue.
2. If the Faroese-taxable ultimate parent meets §118c, record its reporting obligation.

3. For a Faroese constituent entity that is not the ultimate parent, apply §118d: local filing can arise where the parent has no home-country reporting duty, the required automatic CbCR exchange arrangement is absent despite an international tax-information agreement, or a systemic failure has been notified. Preserve evidence of the actual trigger; a general tax treaty is insufficient.

4. Evaluate surrogate relief under §118e. The surrogate jurisdiction must require reporting, have the prescribed exchange arrangements, have no systemic failure or no notification of that failure to the constituent, and receive the required surrogate notification; the Faroese constituent must also notify TAKS. The surrogate must actually file the group report in its home jurisdiction. Keep filing, exchange and notification evidence together.

5. Where multiple Faroese entities face local filing, document the §118d(2) selection and notification of the reporting entity. The statutory wording refers to one or two triggering conditions; if all three arise, obtain an interpretation rather than silently extending it.
6. Maintain separate report and notification tasks. Foreign reporting does not by itself discharge the Faroese notification obligation. [§§118c–f][law]

**Local-filing threshold boundary:** §118c expressly states the prior-year revenue threshold; §118d does not repeat it. TAKS describes the regime using the group threshold. For a foreign-parent case below or near that threshold, or a mismatch between home-country and Faroese thresholds, obtain a documented application of the rules rather than infer an unconditional local-filing exemption. [Tax Act][law]; [TAKS][taks]
### What to compile

Regulation §4 and its annex require three tables: jurisdiction totals, constituent entities/activities, and explanatory information. Keep related-party and independent-party revenue separate. The revenue definition excludes intra-group payments treated as dividends in the payer's jurisdiction. Cash tax includes withholding paid by others on the entity's income; current-year accrued tax excludes deferred tax and provisions for uncertain tax liabilities. These are distinct measures. [Regulation §4(2)][regulation]

Use consistent employee/FTE methodology across years and entities. Tangible assets exclude cash and financial assets. Allocate PE assets to the PE jurisdiction; the regulation separately addresses PE capital and retained earnings. Do not mechanically allocate every PE field in the same way. [§4(2)(6)–(9)][regulation]

The workpaper should reconcile each table row to source accounts and tax records, explain currency and perimeter choices, and identify every adjustment. Do not equate the sum of jurisdiction revenue rows with consolidated revenue without explaining consolidation eliminations.
## Deadlines and filing

For a calendar 2026 report, the statutory twelve-month deadline is **31 December 2027**. The notification belongs to **2026**, before year-end; do not delay it until the report deadline. [§§118c and 118f][law]

Notification identifies the reporting entity, address, tax jurisdiction and registration/V-number or foreign TIN where applicable. Faroese, Danish and English notifications are permitted. Cessation of the reporting duty also requires notification. [Regulation §§1–3][regulation]

TAKS publishes reporting and notification templates. Its guidance accepts the report through a secure delivery route and requires a power of attorney where a third party files. Retrieve the current templates, agree the secure route and preserve receipts. No transmission was tested for this Guide. [TAKS][taks]

If a parent refuses information needed for local filing, the regulation requires the constituent to request it, report the information it has obtained or collected, and notify the authority of the refusal. Missing access is not a licence to omit the filing silently. [Regulation §4(5)][regulation]
## Penalties and interest

Section 139c, items 1–2, provides for a fine for intentional or grossly negligent failure to deliver the report under §§118c–e on time, or for false or misleading information in it. The provision does not state a monetary amount. Do not infer a fixed fine from this Guide. Notification-specific exposure and current penalty practice remain to be checked separately. [Tax Act §139c][law]
## Cross-border points

Retain evidence for the exact counterpart jurisdiction and reporting period. TAKS links the OECD activated-exchange list, but this Guide has not verified any bilateral route. Do not substitute OECD membership, signature of a multilateral agreement or a generic treaty for effective exchange coverage. The complete §118e conditions control the surrogate analysis. [Tax Act][law]; [TAKS][taks]

### 1. Prior-year boundary

Assume a Faroese ultimate parent, a DKK-denominated calendar-year group and no threshold-conversion issue. Verified 2025 consolidated revenue of DKK 5,600,000,000 meets the threshold for the 2026 report. DKK 5,599,999,999 is one krone below it. This tests §118c only, not every foreign-parent local-filing scenario.

Assume a jurisdiction row has DKK 12 million of cash income tax plus DKK 2 million of qualifying withholding paid on its income. Cash tax is DKK 14 million. Its current-year tax expense is independently established at DKK 15 million; DKK 3 million deferred tax and DKK 1 million uncertain-tax provision are excluded from that accrued measure. ### Domestic source and PE screening

Tax Act §2 limits nonresident liability to its listed income, with only expenses incurred to earn that income deductible under subsection 2. The categories include royalties from the Faroes, business participation through a Faroese permanent establishment, Faroese property income, dividends/issuer repurchases and the specified securities disposals. Do not treat that expense rule as allowing net taxation where a specific gross levy such as royalty tax applies. Identify the precise category and then its computation law. [Tax Act §2(1)(c)–(g), (m), (2)][tax]; [Assessment Act §7][rate]

Section 2(3)'s more-than-30-day construction, new-build, installation or assembly rule also covers the specified associated activities. Thirty days exactly does not satisfy that particular duration test, but it does not establish an exemption from §2's other routes. Keep contracts, project dates, sites, personnel and connected activities. A treaty can limit the domestic result only after its actual scope and PE provisions have been established. The ordinary fixed-place/attribution method follows below; agency tests, aggregation and exclusions need the actual applicable instrument. [Tax Act §2(1)(d), (3)][tax]

TAKS explains that domestic fixed-place interpretation follows the treaty concept, referring to Nordic Article 5 and listing management premises, a branch, office, factory, workshop and extraction site. Establish an actual place and business activity; this list alone does not decide an agency or treaty exception. Once a branch PE is established, attribute the income it would earn as an independent enterprise dealing at arm's length with its head enterprise. Include connected asset gains/losses and deduct only expenses incurred to earn the Faroese taxable income. Build an evidenced bridge from attributable third-party receipts, direct costs and supportable head-office allocations, then the Faroese tax adjustments. This is a profit-attribution working paper, not a gross-receipts levy. [Tax Act §2(1)(d), (2)][tax]; [TAKS VLS C.2, fixed establishment][residence]

For example, an established ordinary company branch with DKK 1,000,000 attributable receipts, DKK 600,000 deductible direct costs and DKK 100,000 independently supported attributable head-office costs has DKK 300,000 ordinary profit before other tax adjustments, and DKK 54,000 at the qualifying 18% company rate. These allocations are hypothetical proved inputs, not automatic percentage deductions or a method for attributing internal finance/intangibles. Reconcile depreciation, financing limitations and losses under the corporate/TP Guides. [Tax Act §§2(2), 31, 37b][tax]; [Assessment Act §5(2)][rate]
### Royalties and distributions

Classify the contract first. Tax Act §2(1)(c) covers consideration for the use/right to use the stated copyright, films/broadcast material, patents, trademarks, designs, models, plans, secret formula/process and industrial/commercial/scientific experience. It does not turn an outright asset sale or an ordinary service into a royalty merely because intellectual property is involved. TAKS distinguishes a licence from transfer of ownership. Resident royalties are ordinary B-income under §§1, 25; foreign royalties start with the 25% gross charge. [Tax Act §§2(1)(c), 25][tax]; [Assessment Act §7][rate]; [TAKS royalties][royalty]

For a gross contractual royalty, withholding equals gross entitlement × 25%; net equals gross less withholding. For a contract actually guaranteeing a fixed net entitlement and requiring the payer to bear the tax, gross = net / (1 − applicable rate). A gross-up requires the contract and correct legal rate, not an assumption that the payer will bear the recipient's tax. [Assessment Act §7(1)][rate]

Capital Income Act §1(2) broadly defines distributions. Final-liquidation-year distributions follow disposal treatment under §1(3); a capital reduction can receive that treatment with TAKS permission under §1(4). An issuer repurchase ordinarily follows dividend treatment under §5 unless its permission or specific exceptions apply. Fully Faroese-taxable company/fund recipients holding share or contributed capital are exempt under §9(1); foreign recipients cannot claim that domestic full-liability exemption merely because they are companies. Apply the recipient-specific §15 starting rate before verified treaty or other relief. [Capital Income Act §§1, 5, 9, 15][capital]
### Individual exit, deferral and immigration

When an individual becomes tax-resident in Denmark, Greenland or another country, §2a treats the securities as disposed of if their market value exceeds DKK 100,000. Negative-acquisition-basis shares are caught independently. The threshold tests **market value**, not gain; exactly DKK 100,000 does not cross that limb. Compute the overall statutory net gain using the applicable securities basis/FIFO rules and §14 rate. This rule is not evidence of a general company or business-asset exit tax. [Capital Income Act §§2a, 4, 14][capital]

A realisation-basis taxpayer can seek deferral under §§2b–2c. The departure return and securities inventory are due **no later than the departure day**, with adequate security in the form of a bank guarantee matched to the deferred tax. Create both the security-by-security inventory and a deferred-tax balance. Do not label deferral unconditional or replace that deadline with the next ordinary annual return. [§§2a(2), 2b, 2c(1)][capital]

For each later disposal, use the original acquisition basis used in the exit computation, actual sale proceeds and FIFO. For a positive gain, compute the Faroese tax and credit eligible actual foreign tax under the applicable treaty or §19; pay the positive residual and reduce the deferred balance by the payment. If comparing actual proceeds with departure value produces a loss, §2c(3) separately reduces the balance by that loss's Faroese tax value. A foreign deduction of that loss invokes the separate foreign negative-tax-value payment rule; do not ignore it. Actual acquisition-basis losses have §2c(4)'s separate adjustment. Death is treated as disposal of all inventory securities under subsection 5.

**Bounded later-disposal control:** original cost DKK 100,000, departure value DKK 150,000 and initial deferred tax DKK 17,500; later sale DKK 140,000, no foreign tax, no foreign deduction of the value fall, no other inventory securities or prior balance adjustments. Actual gain DKK 40,000 gives DKK 14,000 tax paid and reduces the balance to DKK 3,500. The DKK 10,000 fall from departure value has DKK 3,500 Faroese tax value, reducing the remaining balance to zero. Do not substitute departure value for the original gain basis, or import this fixture into foreign-loss or rising-value cases without the separate §2c computation. For each year with a positive deferred balance, a return with address is due by 1 May of the following year. [§2c][capital]

On return to Faroese tax residence, apply the exit/deferral rules up to the return date for securities still held, then use market value on return as the incoming basis while retaining the actual acquisition date. For other incoming individuals, §2e likewise preserves acquisition date and uses incoming market value. Listed securities use that day's quoted value; unlisted securities start from the company's net asset value at the end of the last accounting period before arrival, unless TAKS approves a better evidenced valuation. [§§2d–2e][capital]

Apply the separate §2f loss restriction: capital-income losses are not deductible to the extent they arise from disposal proceeds below the incoming value established under §2e. The incoming market-value basis is therefore not an unrestricted promise of relief for every later loss. Preserve both the arrival valuation and actual disposal evidence. [Capital Income Act §2f][capital]

Late royalty remittance under Assessment Act §7(2) carries **1% per month from the due date until paid**. Subsection 3 disallows an income-tax deduction for that interest and applies statutory enforcement. The section does not say “per commenced month”; do not substitute the ordinary 0.7% rule. Late dividend withholding carries **0.7% per commenced month** from the due date, including booked interest as specified, and is not deductible. Late separate capital returns attract estimated assessment, a DKK 1,000–5,000 fine and a 2% increase if less than seven days late or 5% if at least seven days late, with supported application relief under §18(7). [Capital Income Act §§15(4), 18(1), (7)][capital]

Missing the departure return/inventory deadline forfeits deferral and gives **0.7% per commenced month** from the tax's original due date, unless TAKS waives the deadline under §2b(5). Tax Act §141(1)(2)–(3) provides a fine for intentional or grossly negligent failure to withhold/remit royalties or supply the specified §§118–124 information. ## Cross-border points

For each payment or migration event, record domestic residence/source, counterparty and beneficial-owner identity, treaty residence, the treaty actually in force for that date, income article and PE connection, domestic starting tax, entitlement to relief and procedure. A country on an authority list does not by itself establish that a payment is exempt. Do not apply EU directives or Danish domestic rules without Faroese authority.
Controlled-transaction pricing and thin capitalisation belong to the separate TP Guide. [Tax Act §§37a–37b][tax]

**Ordinary corporate-loan interest:** a non-bank Faroese company paying genuine loan interest to a foreign company with no Faroese full liability, PE connection or other domestic taxable connection has no withholding imposed by the cited ordinary royalty, distribution or bank-deposit provisions. This is an inference from their defined scope, not a treaty-granted zero rate: Tax Act §2 exhaustively lists nonresident income categories without a general loan-interest category; Assessment Act §7 covers royalties; Capital Income Act §15 covers distributions; §16 covers interest credited by Faroese banks/postgiro to individuals/estates. Thus DKK 20,000 genuine interest in that bounded fixture is paid DKK 20,000 without those withholdings. A disguised distribution, bank deposit, PE-connected debt, different recipient or special instrument requires its own classification; §16's 35% bank-deposit withholding must not be described as a general corporate-interest rate. [Tax Act §2][tax]; [Assessment Act §7][rate]; [Capital Income Act §§2, 15–16][capital]; [TAKS VLS C.2][residence]
### Ordinary foreign-tax credit

For foreign ordinary income from a country **without a double-tax treaty**, Tax Act §154 allows credit for foreign income tax actually paid or withheld, limited to Faroese tax attributable to the same income. Capital Income Act §19 supplies the separate capital-income rule. Include the eligible foreign income in the correct Faroese base before relief. For a positive ordinary worldwide base, the ordinary limit is `Faroese income tax before foreign relief × eligible net foreign income / worldwide taxable income in that calculation`; credit is the lower of that limit and eligible foreign tax. This is a credit from tax, not a second deduction of the foreign tax from the income base. [Tax Act §§25, 154][tax]; [Capital Income Act §19][capital]; [TAKS VLS O.1.1–O.1.4][relief]

Use only income and tax belonging to the same calculation. Deduct foreign-related expenses from the foreign numerator; allocate expenses relating to both sources proportionally to their gross income. Keep countries separate, and separate income types where methods or tax calculations differ. Special-rate income has its own computed-tax cap. Retain source-income, expense and paid/withheld-tax evidence. Treaty entitlement, losses or a nonpositive denominator, tax changes/refunds, unused-credit treatment and return-field implementation require their own checks. [TAKS VLS O.1.3–O.1.7][relief]

For individuals, TAKS distinguishes ordinary tax credits from refundable child credit: ordinary credits are allocated before foreign relief as described in O.1.8, while child credit follows relief and retains its statutory refund treatment. Relief is allocated proportionally between national, municipal and church tax under O.1.9. Do not copy the older guidance's illustrative bands or foreign-work deduction amounts into a 2026 calculation; use the current income-tax Guides and the actual treaty where relevant. # Faroe Islands individual income tax v0.5

> **Checked against the law.** This Guide prepares income-year 2026 working papers. Selected current law and authority tables were read on 25 October 2026, with the church-tax, spouse and bounded part-year methods checked on 28 October; professional review is pending.
## Who this applies to

Faroese domestic full liability arises from a home under Tax Act §1(1)(1), or, without a home, a stay of at least **180 days in a twelve-month period**, interrupted or not, under §1(1)(4). Exactly 180 meets that stay test; fewer days do not disprove the separate home test. Other statutory routes include specified students/apprentices abroad and seafarers. Determine commencement/cessation and treaty residence separately. Fully liable persons start with worldwide income under §25; nonresidents are limited to §2 categories. [Tax Act §§1–2, 25][tax]

Employees, sole traders, partners, investors and landlords require different schedules. Spouses are individually assessed under §4; allocate a joint business by actual participation and spouse remuneration by actual work. The municipal allowance equalisation in §4(1) is not general joint national-rate taxation. Children are separately taxable subject to §5's family-business wage and gifted-asset-income rules. [Tax Act §§4–5][tax]
Do not import Danish tax bands, an automatic 183-day exemption or a universal net-pay percentage. Pensions, social charges and separate capital tax require their own bases.

### Ordinary income and deductions

Build separate schedules for wages/benefits, business profit, rents, foreign income and investments. Use the payroll Guide’s [dated 2026 benefit-value schedule](fo-payroll-contributions.md#ordinary-benefit-valuation) for ordinary housing, utilities, meals and cars, with its stated adjustment/exemption limits. A/B classification determines collection, not a new exemption. Tax Act §§57, 60–62 define the routes; doubt about classification is decided by TAKS under §62(2). Ordinary wage/A-income timing generally follows payment, with §28's backstop at the end of the following calendar year and acceleration when liability ceases. [Tax Act §§25, 28, 57, 60–62][tax]

For business profit, reconcile sales and expenses, remove private withdrawals/use, correct inventory and replace accounting depreciation with the statutory asset schedule. Section 31 permits expenses incurred to earn, secure and maintain business income but expressly excludes ordinary expenses of earning A-income/personal employment income. Do not deduct an employee's ordinary work costs as sole-trader costs. Business interest/finance costs follow §33(1)(1), including its unpaid-interest clawback. Pre-trading research expenditure has the separate §32 start-year/next-three-years rule. Carry business losses under §33a only when not usable earlier; debt-release loss reductions must be applied. [Tax Act §§26, 31–33a][tax]

Equipment depreciation requires the Depreciation Act classification, pool, disposal and private-use rules. The ordinary exclusive-business pool maximum is 30%; qualifying items or positive pool remainders of DKK 20,000 or less have separate immediate-deduction rules. Keep the underlying asset evidence; the corporate Guide's [asset schedules](fo-corporate-income-tax.md) explain these shared provisions, without applying its company rate to a person. [Depreciation Act §§1–8][depreciation]

Before finalising an individual's depreciation or investment-fund deduction, apply Tax Act §31(2)–(6)'s separate **personal-consumption floor**. If taxable income is below the statutory consumption computation, increase income toward that amount, but by no more than the depreciation/investment-fund deductions covered by the rule. Section 31(4) excludes year-bound depreciation that would otherwise be lost. Under §31(5), the denied depreciation is treated as not taken in that year; preserve it in the asset records instead of losing it or deducting it twice. For spouses, the statutory consumption calculation includes both spouses' full-year income and opening/closing assets and liabilities. This floor is distinct from an asset's private-use adjustment. Obtain the actual consumption working paper before confirming the base. [Tax Act §31(2)–(6)][tax]

Regulation 98/1987 §1 gives the ordinary indirect consumption calculation: opening net assets plus taxable income, asset increases outside taxable income, deductions that did not reduce assets and nontaxable valuation increases; subtract non-consumption asset reductions not deducted in arriving at income, taxable income that did not increase assets, nondeductible valuation decreases and closing net assets. Reconcile each component. A direct calculation is permitted where acceptable annual accounts include all income/expenses and opening/closing assets/liabilities. Apply §2's particular spouse, separation and death rules rather than mechanically combining every household. [Regulation 98/1987 §§1–3][consumption]

Eligible paid pension contributions have deduction/exclusion under Pension Act §12(3)–(4) in the year contributed, including the specified voluntary payments. Do not deduct the same payment twice. The pension contribution itself has a separate pension tax under §12(2)/annex 1, with provisional 40% withholding and final income-linked rates; a personal income-tax deduction does not make the pension payment tax-free. Mandatory contribution funding, exceptions and collection are in the [payroll Guide](fo-payroll-contributions.md). [Pension Act §§2, 12 and annex 1][pension]
### Family, municipality and ceiling

For a full-year cohabiting spouse case under §4, first establish each spouse's own taxable income. Where the lower nonnegative income is below DKK 30,000 and the other is above it, the ordinary adjustment transfers the unused amount: `transfer = 30,000 − lower income`; raise the lower income to DKK 30,000 and reduce the higher income by that transfer. TAKS expressly illustrates DKK 20,000 / 300,000 becoming DKK 30,000 / 290,000, and DKK 0 / 300,000 becoming DKK 30,000 / 270,000, automatically at year-end. Keep the spouses separately assessed on the adjusted bases. This bounded method does not settle negative-income, separation, death or part-year spouse cases. [Tax Act §4][tax]; [TAKS spouse adjustment][spouse]

For national child credit, establish full liability, required residence, custody/child's home, child age on 1 January and child's Faroese residence or retained full liability while studying abroad. Apply the recipient/transfer rules and proportional reduction where the recipient's liability covers only part of the year. A child taken into statutory care ends entitlement. The credit reduces tax, not taxable income; an excess is refundable under §2(3). [Assessment Act §2][rate]

Determine the tax municipality under §§41–44, ordinarily residence on 1 December before the income year, with commencement/move rules. Apply the current municipal child credit separately from the national amount. TAKS explains the written agreement/preliminary-registration process for transferring or sharing eligible credit and the refund treatment where credit exceeds tax. Preserve the actual allocation rather than giving both parents the full credit. Pensioner national credits have separate eligibility under Assessment Act §3; unused credit transfers to municipal tax only up to that tax under Tax Act §47(2). [Tax Act §§41–47][tax]; [Assessment Act §§2–3][rate]; [TAKS child credit][child]

For municipal calculation, §47 directs rounding taxable income down to a multiple of DKK 100 before computing the tax. Keep that rounding distinct from payment rounding. Compute each national/municipal/church component, eligible credits and the §54(2) proportional ceiling adjustment in a traceable schedule. The ceiling does not establish a 50% limit on every tax, contribution and pension outflow together. Use the bounded part-year method below; unusual credit/ceiling interactions require the additional checks listed in Sources. [Tax Act §§24(2), 46–47, 54(2)][tax]

For an ordinary full-year church member, calculate church tax on the ordinary municipal income base **after the DKK 30,000 exempt amount**, using the actual parish rate. Church Finance Act §§11–13 separates national and local church rates and uses the municipal collection rules. The official 2024 audit report expressly confirms that TAKS calculates church tax in the same way as municipal tax, deducting the municipal exempt amount first. Read with Tax Act §§46–47, the working-paper base is `max(income rounded down to DKK 100 − 30,000, 0)`. Apply the church rate to that base separately; a municipal child credit does not reduce the base. The report also records the Finance Ministry's explanation that the special 42%/35% limited-liability gross levy does not attract an additional church charge. This full-year method does not settle changes of membership during a year, part-year allowances or final sub-krone settlement rounding. [Church Finance Act §§11–14][church]; [Tax Act §§46–47][tax]; [Landsgrannskoðanin, 2024 report §4.10, pp. 44–46][church-audit]; [2026 parish rates][municipal]
### Ordinary arrival and departure during the year

Liability continues while the statutory residence/source conditions are met. Acquiring a home without actually taking up residence does not itself start the home-based route; the 180-day stay route instead starts retrospectively from the first qualifying arrival. Preserve the actual home, arrival/departure and presence evidence. A registration date alone does not decide tax residence. A home retained after departure requires the actual facts to be assessed. [Tax Act §§1, 6–8][tax]; [TAKS VLS C.1][residence]

For a bounded 2026 ordinary resident period with no credits, church membership, foreign relief, spouse transfer or special-rate income, §24(2) requires conversion to full-year income. The TAKS 2026 calculator demonstrates the administrative sequence: actual taxable income × `365 / taxable days`, rounded down to DKK 100; compute the current full-year national and municipal taxes on that annualised base, then multiply their sum by `taxable days / 365`. The municipal exempt amount is applied in the annual calculation before this reduction. Treat this as the observed calculator working-paper method, not an express statutory rounding rule for every component. [Tax Act §§24(2), 46–47][tax]; [TAKS calculator guidance][calculator-info]; [TAKS 2026 calculator][calculator]

**Observed control, not a client assessment:** for DKK 150,000 income over 180 taxable days in Tórshavn, without church tax or any credit, the official calculator shows annualised income DKK 304,100, gross annual tax DKK 85,644 and reduced tax DKK 42,235.40; its final income-tax display is DKK 42,235. The unrounded annual equivalent is DKK 304,166.67. This recomputes as national DKK 33,565 plus municipal DKK 52,079, then ×180/365. Its separately displayed 3% AM charge is DKK 4,500 on actual income. The calculator is expressly indicative. Its displayed child-credit amount differs from the current Assessment Act, so no child-credit result is adopted from it. Part-year credits, spouse cases, changing church membership and final settlement rounding remain separate questions. [Assessment Act §§1–2][rate]; [TAKS calculator][calculator]
### Capital income, rentals and interest support

Separate non-business securities/claims/debt/options/dividends/interest under the Capital Income Act. Securities gains generally use realised proceeds less acquisition basis and FIFO for equal-right shares; business-related investments instead follow §3's ordinary-income route, subject to its irrevocable mark-to-market election. For individuals, §6(4)'s DKK 1,000 annual claim/debt-gain threshold and listed-instrument loss condition are specific rules, not a general allowance against all share gains. Private interest income enters the separate §14 computation under §10, subject to express exemptions. [Capital Income Act §§1, 3–10][capital]

Aggregate eligible §14 categories, carry unused capital losses to the earliest available future capital net gains, and apply 35% to a positive balance. Do not deduct a private capital loss against salary. Reconcile dividend/bank-interest withholding and the separate assessment under §§15–18 instead of taxing the same receipt twice. Pension-scheme investments excluded by §1(5) are not an ordinary private portfolio. Gifts, inheritance and family succession have separate §§11–13 rules. [Capital Income Act §§1, 11–18][capital]

Residential rent can follow ordinary accounts or the §8a gross election. The DKK 100,000 allowance is combined where there are co-owners, and the election binds for three years. TAKS requires qualifying direct residential letting for at least three months with the tenant actually resident; do not extend the election to short-stay tourism. Ordinary rental accounts require their own expense and asset schedules. [Assessment Act §8a][rate]; [TAKS housing/rents][rent]

For personal housing/student/other specified borrowing, the separate Interest Support Act supplies relief instead of a general private-interest deduction. Establish full liability and the actual loan purpose/date, qualifying own home and ownership. Home support is capped per property and commissions are excluded. Mixed home/business property is expressly treated under this Act by §2a; mixed-purpose loans must first be split. Negative loan interest reduces eligible expense, and double reimbursement is prohibited. Apply on the required form with bank evidence; the ordinary own-home formula is min(eligible interest, 100,000) × 35%, subject to all eligibility rules. Student loans and older borrowing do not automatically share that property cap. [Interest Support Act §§1–8][support]
### Special work categories

Screen foreign-work §25b income and its exclusions before applying Assessment Act §1(2)'s 35% route. For 2026, Tax Act §33(1)(13) allows its 30% deduction capped at DKK 48,000, subject to §33(2)'s transitional maximum DKK 96,000 for the stated 2024 Nordic-relief population. The distinct foreign-work expense allowance under §33(1)(12) is DKK 120 per qualifying day in 2026, with its two-continuous-month/100-day stay tests and income cap; do not stack it onto excluded §25b income. [Tax Act §§25b, 33(1)(12)–(13), (2)][tax]; [Assessment Act §1(2)][rate]

The statutory fishing-income deduction is 14% of qualifying catch income up to DKK 300,000 under §33(1)(17). Qualifying apprentices have up to DKK 50,000 annual deduction, proportional to qualifying days, under §33(1)(19); an ordinary student internship is not an apprenticeship. FAS/DIS, frontier work, overseas public service and treaty exemptions still require their own facts and authority. [Tax Act §33(1)(17), (19)][tax]
## Deadlines and filing

Ordinary individual returns are due **1 May following the income year**, subject to the specified §100(3) exceptions, including its §2 nonresident category deadline. A correct and complete issued statement can remove the separate return requirement under §101(2); an absent form does not. A permitted extension cannot pass **15 August** under §105. Self-employed accounts and the applicable property statement accompany filing, with accounts submitted on Borgaragluggin. For ordinary calendar-year 2026 resident filing, the starting date is 1 May 2027; verify the actual issued assessment and any extension. [Tax Act §§100–105][tax]; [TAKS returns][returns]

Update preliminary registration where expected income changes. B-tax is ordinarily due on the first of each month, payable through the 20th, with weekend/public-holiday extension; if annual B-tax is **below** DKK 1,000, two instalments fall on 1 June and 1 December under §74. Extra voluntary preliminary payment can be made by **31 January** of the assessment year under §76. [Tax Act §§67–76][tax]

Reconcile final tax with A/B and voluntary payments under §77. Ordinary residual tax carries a **4% supplement**; the usual assessed schedule is three equal instalments due 1 May/June/July, payable through the 20th, with the small-balance and later-issued assessment rules in §78. A balance including supplement of DKK 100 or less is not collected; DKK 1,000 or less uses the specified single-instalment route. Follow the actual assessment rather than inventing monthly deductions after year-end. [Tax Act §§77–80][tax]

Separate capital reporting follows §18 and the applicable ordinary return deadline; a correct complete issued capital statement needs no additional form. Capital residual tax of DKK 500 or less is not collected and refunds below DKK 50 are not paid. Those are settlement thresholds, not investment-gain exemptions. Tax is due the first of the month after assessment, payable through the 20th. [Capital Income Act §18][capital]
## Penalties and interest

A missing/late complete ordinary return permits estimated assessment, a DKK 1,000–5,000 fine, and tax increases of 2% if less than seven days late or 5% if at least seven days late. Section 104(3) permits relief on supported application, not automatically. Late tax/preliminary tax carries **0.7% per commenced month** from the due date under §135. Separate capital-return/payment rules are in Capital Income Act §18, including the corresponding late-return fine/increases and 0.7% monthly payment interest. [Tax Act §§104, 135][tax]; [Capital Income Act §18][capital]

False/misleading information with evasion intent is subject to Tax Act §139 fine, detention or up to two years' imprisonment, with separate gross-negligence treatment. Sections 139a–141 cover specified statement corrections, nonfiling and information/control failures. No fixed offence fine is invented here. Distinguish the §78 residual-tax supplement from late-payment interest or an offence penalty. [Tax Act §§78, 139–141][tax]
## Cross-border points

Classify domestic versus treaty residence, work location, payer, actual days, income article and relief evidence. The 42% A-income-only nonresident rule does not govern every foreign person's Faroese property/business income. A stay below 180 days does not itself prove treaty exemption. Tax Act §1(3) restricts deductions for a treaty-foreign resident to expenses concerning income the Faroes may tax. [Tax Act §§1–2][tax]; [Assessment Act §§1, 8][rate]

Capital Income Act §19 permits capped foreign-tax credit for capital income from a country **without** a double-tax treaty. Tax Act §154 supplies the separate ordinary-income credit; the [cross-border Guide’s bounded method](fo-cross-border-payments.md#ordinary-foreign-tax-credit) explains source expenses, the positive-base fraction and credit ordering. Treaty credits/exemptions, nonpositive bases and the other stated limits require their own authority; do not use §19 as a universal credit rule. Individual securities departure/entry and deferral are covered in the [cross-border Guide](fo-cross-border-payments.md). [Capital Income Act §§2a–2f, 19][capital]

### 1. Ordinary full-year resident

Assume a full-year adult resident in Tórshavnar, no church membership, child/pensioner credit or special income, and established ordinary taxable income DKK 300,000 after base adjustments. National tax is DKK 32,950 and municipal tax DKK 51,300, total DKK 84,250. This is income tax, not take-home pay or total pension/social charges. # Faroe Islands payroll and mandatory contributions v0.3

> **Checked against the law.** Income year 2026; selected current statutes and authority guidance read 25 October 2026; benefit, dated pension and contribution provisions re-read 28 October 2026. This Guide prepares payroll working papers, with professional review pending.
## Who this applies to

Apply to payers of Faroese A-income, employees and self-employed persons where each named contribution applies. Wages, holiday pay, board fees, specified replacement benefits and employer cash gifts have A-income classification under Tax Act §60. A foreign payer, a statutory exception or non-cash benefit needs its own classification; §62 makes TAKS the decision-maker in doubt. The distinction is not settled by a payslip label. [Tax Act §§57, 60–62][tax]

Before paying A-income, route it through an authorised settlement institution under §63. Supply the payee's P-tal/temporary identification, name/address, earnings period and amount, and deliver the statutory written payslip information with each payment. Reconcile the institution's itemised tax withholding to the wage ledger. A tax computed from annual bands alone is not a substitute for the live cumulative withholding instruction. [Tax Act §§63–64][tax]

Income tax, statutory worker charges, employer charges, pension funding and holiday entitlement are separate. An employee-side age or foreign-coverage exception does not automatically exempt the employer. A pension contribution transferred by the employer is not necessarily an additional employer-funded benefit: establish the employment contract and statutory minimum separately. [Pension Act §§1–3][pension]; [AMEG Act §2][ameg]; [ALS Act §§7–9][als]; [Parental Act §§17–19][parental]
